title: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity
text: From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity. November 25, 2026 Science From spectrum to structure: Identifying molecules with Mass Spec Skills for Google Antigravity Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Explore Science on Google Antigravity Share Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. title: Migrating our Messages API to Rust
text: Migrating our Messages API to Rust. 01 Why migrate? Related articles Effective harnesses for long-running agents View more Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work. But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite , and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything . Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it. We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities
text: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities. OpenAI November 24, 2026 Science Publication GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities Read the paper (opens in a new window) Share Key findings: Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs. An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take. In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing. The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules. In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools. Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. text: Searching for distant planets with Astra. OpenAI An illustrated view of HD 164604 b zooms out to the Milky Way. Boxes mark a selection of systems with confirmed exoplanets. Distances are scaled to the zoom and show the distance from Earth at the widest view. Hover over or tap a box to read its label. Use the arrow keys to browse labels and Escape to dismiss them. November 24, 2026 Science Searching for distant planets with Astra Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely. Share Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system ⁠ (opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992 ⁠ (opens in a new window) . A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers. *Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table ⁠ (opens in a new window) . 2026 data are year to date through November 24, 2026. How astronomers discover exoplanets Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope ⁠ (opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. title: Introducing Make Endpoints
text: Introducing Make Endpoints. Release notes 2026 Introducing Make Endpoints 2 min Make Endpoints lets developers call supported app actions from JavaScript, TypeScript, or REST while keeping application logic in their own code. Use team-managed Make connections to run each action and receive its output directly. ﻿ What's new Direct app actions: Call supported app actions without creating a one-step scenario for each request. JavaScript, TypeScript, and REST support: Use generated, typed SDK clients for supported actions or call Endpoints through REST from other stacks. Managed connections: Pass a compatible Make connection ID when required. Provider credentials remain in the Make connection, not in your request input. Endpoint discovery: Check available Endpoints through team-scoped discovery and inspect SDK definitions with the `make-endpoints-cli`. Not every Make app has Endpoints, and CLI output does not confirm that a compatible team connection is available. Agent tools: Use EndpointTools to create JavaScript or TypeScript tool definitions for selected Endpoints. Endpoint logs dashboard in Make: Open the team-level Endpoint logs page to see when each call ran, which app and Endpoint it used, its status, user, connection ID, and duration. Filter the list and open Details to investigate a call. Beta pricing: Each Endpoint call costs 0.1 Make credit during beta. ﻿ Availability: Available on all Make plans, including Free.
